summary: Second Peter 1 opens by naming Simon Peter and blessing readers who share a precious faith. The chapter moves from God's provision to the readers' active growth, then to a farewell-like reminder and a claim that the message about Jesus rests on eyewitness testimony and the prophetic word.
whyItMatters: This chapter sets the letter's main concerns: knowledge joined to conduct, remembering what has already been taught, and confidence in testimony rather than invented stories. It also introduces the disputed question of authorship because the writing speaks in Peter's voice while later readers differ about whether the apostle himself wrote it.

context.author: The address names Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ. Traditional attribution accepts Peter as author; many modern critical scholars regard the work as a later writing in his name.
context.audience: Believers described as having obtained a faith of equal value with the writer's; their destination is not named.
context.date: Disputed. Petrine authorship places it in the apostolic period, while many scholars who favor a later author propose the early second century.
context.setting: The place of writing and the readers' location are not stated. The chapter presents a speaker who expects his death soon and wants his readers to remember what they know.
context.literaryForm: Exhortation framed as a letter and farewell reminder, moving from greeting to moral appeal to testimony about Jesus and prophecy.

outline.heading: Greeting and shared faith
outline.note: Simon Peter addresses readers who share a precious faith and blesses them with grace and peace through knowledge of God and Jesus.

outline.heading: Divine provision and promises
outline.note: The chapter says divine power has granted what pertains to life and godliness, along with promises through which readers may share in the divine nature and escape corruption.

outline.heading: A linked pattern of growth
outline.note: Readers are urged to supply faith with moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love, with the promise of stability and entrance into the eternal Kingdom.

outline.heading: Reminder before departure
outline.note: The speaker says he will keep reminding readers, even though they know the truth, because his departure is near.

outline.heading: Eyewitnesses and the prophetic word
outline.note: The chapter contrasts the message with cunningly devised fables, recalls the voice heard on the holy mountain, and says prophecy came as holy men were moved by the Holy Spirit.

keyVerses.text: seeing that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue,
keyVerses.why: This verse grounds the appeal in what God has already granted, not only in what the readers must do.

keyVerses.text: Yes, and for this very cause adding on your part all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge;
keyVerses.why: This begins the chain of qualities that shapes the chapter's call to active growth.

keyVerses.text: For we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter's claim that the message about Jesus is not invented but tied to witness.

keyVerses.text: For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.
keyVerses.why: This closes the chapter by explaining prophecy as something grounded in God's action rather than human initiative.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter opens with the name Simon Peter and identifies him as a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ. That is the writing's own presentation. Readers differ on whether the apostle Peter himself wrote the letter or whether a later writer composed it in Peter's name.

questions.question: Who are the readers?
questions.answer: The chapter addresses people who have obtained a faith described as like precious with the writer's. It does not name a city, region, or congregation. The readers already know the teaching being recalled, because the writer says they are established in the present truth.

questions.question: What does “divine nature” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase describes sharing in God's life through his promises. Here it is linked to escape from the world's corruption and to growth in moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, affection, and love. The immediate emphasis is God's gift expressed in a changed way of life; the verse does not explain a complete theory of participation in the divine nature.

questions.question: Why does the chapter list so many qualities in verses 5-7?
questions.answer: The qualities are linked in a chain: faith, moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. The point is not that one quality must be finished before the next begins. The chapter says these things keep readers from being idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.

questions.question: Does “make your calling and election sure” mean readers create their own election?
questions.answer: The verse tells the readers to be diligent and connects that diligence with not stumbling. In the flow of the chapter, God's power and promises come first, and the readers' effort follows. Interpreters debate how this relates to wider doctrines of grace and assurance, but this chapter itself holds divine provision and active diligence together.

questions.question: What is meant by “tent” and “departure”?
questions.answer: The speaker uses “tent” as an image for his present bodily life. He says the putting off of his tent comes swiftly, and then speaks of his departure. The image explains why he urgently wants the readers to remember these things after he is gone.

questions.question: What event is being recalled on the holy mountain?
questions.answer: This recalls Jesus' Transfiguration. The Gospel accounts describe Peter, James, and John seeing Jesus in glory on a mountain and hearing a heavenly voice identify him as God's beloved Son. Second Peter highlights the witnessed majesty and the voice to support its message about Jesus' power and coming. It gives a brief recollection rather than retelling every detail of the Gospel scene.

questions.question: Does “no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation” forbid individual Bible reading?
questions.answer: The next verse explains the statement by saying prophecy did not come by the will of man, but by holy men moved by the Holy Spirit. Because of that, many readers understand the point to concern the origin of prophecy rather than a complete rule about who may read Scripture. Others connect it more directly with guarding interpretation from private distortion, especially in light of the letter's later warnings.

questions.question: Why contrast eyewitnesses with fables?
questions.answer: The chapter says the message about the power and coming of Jesus Christ did not rest on cunningly devised fables. It then appeals to eyewitnesses of his majesty and to the prophetic word. The contrast prepares readers to value remembered testimony and Scripture as they face disputed teaching later in the letter.

glossary.def: A commissioned representative. In this verse the speaker uses it for his relationship to Jesus Christ.
A life oriented toward God. The chapter says God has granted what pertains to it and then includes it among the qualities readers are to supply.
Steady endurance. It appears in the linked list of qualities between self-control and godliness.
Care within the believing community. It is paired with love at the end of the chain in verses 5-7.
The chapter's image for bodily life that can be put off at death.
Invented stories. The chapter denies that the message about Jesus' power and coming was based on them.

reviewer: Codex editorial panel (2 Peter, Titus, Nahum)
